From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Overall assessment

The package is materially seller-favourable. The principal concern is the interaction between:

1. very broad data-room and public-record disclosure;
2. deemed/constructive Buyer knowledge;
3. a 20% cap and short 18-month claim period;
4. deductible thresholds; and
5. limitations, non-reliance and exclusive remedy provisions applying to **all Claims**.

Together, these provisions could leave Wattlebridge with little or no remedy for several known and potentially material problems. Labelling provisions “[STANDARD]” or “cleared” has no effect and should be disregarded.

The Disclosure Letter is dated by reference to a data-room snapshot at **22 September 2026**, now more than six weeks old. An updated data room, disclosure letter and warranty bring-down will be required.

## Material issues and proposed pushback

### 1. Liability regime is too broad and inadequately calibrated

#### Seller position
- General Warranty Claims capped at AUD 4.8 million.
- AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 deductible basket.
- 18-month limitation period.
- Capacity and title subject to the same regime.
- Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to all Claims.
- Tax and IP also fall within the general regime.

#### Buyer concern
A 20% cap may be negotiable for genuinely general business warranties, but it is unacceptable for title, capacity, tax, specific indemnities, debt and leakage. Applying it to title would mean that if the Seller cannot transfer the shares, the Buyer could pay AUD 24 million but recover only AUD 4.8 million.

An 18-month period may expire before tax audits, IP disputes, regulatory investigations or latent liabilities emerge. Applying limitations to “all Claims” may also unintentionally restrict claims for breach of pre-completion covenants, completion obligations, debt adjustments, leakage, indemnities, fraud or statutory misleading conduct.

#### Pushback
Require separate regimes:

- **Title, capacity and authority:** 100% of the purchase price; at least six years, or no contractual limitation for title.
- **Tax covenant and tax warranties:** 100% cap and seven years or the relevant statutory assessment period plus a buffer.
- **Specific indemnities:** outside the general warranty cap, basket and de minimis, with exposure appropriate to the relevant risk.
- **Debt, leakage, transaction expenses and purchase-price adjustments:** dollar-for-dollar and outside warranty limitations.
- **Fraud, fraudulent concealment, wilful misconduct and deliberate breach:** uncapped and not subject to contractual time or remedy restrictions.
- **Pre-completion covenants and completion obligations:** not treated as general Warranty Claims.
- Preserve statutory and equitable remedies; non-reliance and exclusive-remedy language must not apply universally.

For general warranties, seek a higher cap—commercially at least 30–50% absent warranty and indemnity insurance—and 24–36 months. Ask for a tipping basket rather than recovery only above AUD 250,000, and aggregate related claims for de minimis purposes.

Claim notices should not fail for technical deficiencies, and any notified claim should survive the limitation period until resolved.

---

### 2. General disclosure and constructive knowledge should be rejected

#### Seller position
The Seller purports to disclose the entire data room, accounts, statutory registers and all publicly searchable corporate records. Any matter known to the Buyer or its advisers, or discoverable from those sources, bars a claim.

#### Buyer concern
This shifts the risk of an inadequately organised or ambiguous data room to Wattlebridge. It may permit the Seller to defeat a warranty claim by pointing to a passing reference in an unrelated document. “Discoverable” matters and adviser knowledge create a constructive-knowledge standard broader than actual awareness.

The Disclosure Letter also repeatedly avoids conclusions: it discloses incomplete facts while refusing to state whether consent, notification, remediation or payment is required. That is not adequate disclosure of the nature and scope of an exception.

#### Pushback
- Delete general disclosure of the data room and public records.
- Only matters **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature, scope and reasonably foreseeable consequences** should qualify warranties.
- Each disclosure should identify the particular warranty it qualifies.
- Freeze and attach a complete data-room index and archive.
- Public records should qualify warranties only if specifically identified.
- Buyer knowledge should mean actual knowledge of a short list of named senior deal-team individuals, without attribution of advisers’ knowledge and without any duty to investigate.
- The Seller should bear the burden of proving knowledge or fair disclosure.
- Knowledge should not qualify title, tax covenant, debt/leakage, specific indemnities, fraud or completion obligations.
- Due diligence should not constitute a waiver.

Most importantly, known issues should be addressed through conditions, price mechanics or indemnities, rather than merely being disclosed and thereby transferred to the Buyer.

---

### 3. Bluefen consent must be a genuine condition precedent

Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue**. There is no final consent and no evidence that the conditions in clause 11.3 have been fulfilled.

“Reasonable endeavours” and treating the condition as satisfied upon delivery of a written consent are insufficient. The consent may be conditional, accompanied by adverse pricing changes, or ineffective until further conditions are met.

Require:

- receipt before Completion of unconditional and effective written consent, in a form satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably;
- satisfaction or waiver by Bluefen of every associated condition;
- no material amendment, fee, concession, termination right or adverse change without Buyer consent;
- the condition to be waivable only by the Buyer;
- information and consultation rights while consent is pursued; and
- termination rights at the long-stop date.

If the Seller cannot obtain a clean consent, the Buyer should be free not to complete or to renegotiate price/protection.

---

### 4. Riverlark debt and security must be discharged at Completion

A release “following Completion” is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free acquisition. Wattlebridge should not acquire shares in a company that remains liable for AUD 3.2 million or whose assets remain secured.

Require, as Completion deliverables:

- an agreed payout letter;
- repayment from Seller proceeds or a corresponding reduction in consideration;
- an effective release of the Company, its assets and guarantees;
- control of all PPSR and other security discharge documents;
- release of any guarantees, indemnities, cash collateral or account controls; and
- an irrevocable undertaking for any purely administrative registration completed after Completion.

Completion should not occur merely on a promise to provide releases later.

---

### 5. Completion bonuses are Seller transaction expenses

The AUD 420,000 bonuses arise because of Completion. Continued-employment conditions may cause the legal payment date to fall after Completion, but that does not make them a Buyer cost.

The current treatment also ignores payroll tax, superannuation, leave interactions and other on-costs.

Require:

- the bonuses and all associated taxes and on-costs to be treated as Seller transaction expenses/debt-like items;
- payment or full funding through the Completion funds flow;
- no double counting in working capital;
- a dollar-for-dollar indemnity for any post-Completion liability; and
- Seller responsibility for related employee communications and approvals.

The funds flow should be revised before signing.

---

### 6. Ironquay creates an unresolved IP title risk

Transfer of the SOW3 project materials is conditional on payment, and AUD 180,000 remains recorded as open. For an analytics business, an incomplete IP chain of title is potentially fundamental.

The proposed indemnity limited to “the specific SOW3 payment” is inadequate. The Buyer’s loss could include inability to use or commercialise software, infringement claims, customer remediation and business interruption, well beyond AUD 180,000.

Require before Completion:

- evidence of cleared payment;
- a receipt and unconditional confirmatory assignment/release from Ironquay;
- confirmation that all relevant deliverables, source code and associated IP are included; and
- verification that no other fees, liens or retained rights exist.

Also require a specific indemnity covering all losses arising from deficient ownership or transfer of the relevant IP, outside the general warranty limitations. Broader IP warranties should have a separate, longer and higher-cap regime rather than the 20%/18-month general regime.

---

### 7. Privacy/data incident needs active remediation and a specific indemnity

The disclosure leaves unresolved:

- whether the download link was accessed;
- the full dataset and affected individuals;
- containment and deletion;
- whether an eligible data breach or other notification obligation arose;
- customer contractual obligations; and
- regulatory or third-party exposure.

The description as “preliminary” and “not expected to be material” is not evidence.

Before Completion, require:

- a privileged forensic and legal assessment;
- access, download and deletion logs;
- identification of affected records and recipients;
- documented containment and remediation;
- analysis of OAIC, affected-person, customer and contractual notification requirements;
- prompt notice to and consultation with the Buyer;
- preservation of insurance rights and evidence; and
- no notification or admission without consultation, except where legally required.

Seek a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the pre-Completion incident, including investigation, remediation, notification, customer claims, regulatory action and reasonable professional costs. Consider a retention or escrow until the investigation and notification analysis are complete.

---

### 8. Supplier renewals require financial and contractual analysis

The three AUD 110,000 renewals should not simply be declared ordinary-course costs. The documents do not establish whether they are binding, terminable, prepaid, accrued, avoidable or outside historical practice.

Require confirmation of:

- contract terms, renewal periods and termination rights;
- whether commitments were entered into consistently with prior practice;
- accounting treatment in working capital and debt;
- whether any amount is overdue or prepaid; and
- whether the contracts overlap or reflect related suppliers.

Material new commitments between signing and Completion should require Buyer consent. Properly accrued ordinary-course expenses can remain within working-capital mechanics, but transaction-driven, overdue or exceptional commitments should not be transferred without adjustment.

---

### 9. Tax protection cannot sit under the general warranty regime

A 20% cap and 18-month period are unsuitable for pre-Completion tax liabilities, which commonly emerge after the general warranty period.

Require a standalone tax covenant covering all tax attributable to pre-Completion periods and Seller-group arrangements, together with:

- a 100% cap or equivalent purchase-price protection;
- a limitation period tied to statutory assessment periods;
- protection for payroll tax, superannuation, employment taxes and bonus on-costs;
- control and cooperation provisions for tax claims; and
- carefully limited exclusions, including no exclusion merely because material appeared in due diligence.

---

### 10. Title requires warranties and Completion evidence, not merely a register

A company share register is relevant evidence but does not prove beneficial ownership, valid issue, absence of encumbrances or lack of third-party rights.

Require warranties that:

- the Seller is the sole legal and beneficial owner;
- the shares are validly issued and fully paid;
- no option, trust, security interest, pre-emption right or other third-party right exists;
- all corporate approvals have been obtained; and
- the Seller has full power to transfer good title.

Completion deliverables should include executed transfers, original certificates or satisfactory lost-certificate arrangements, updated registers, necessary releases and corporate approvals. These matters must not be qualified by general disclosure or the Buyer’s knowledge.

---

### 11. Office lease and Mossvale should be confirmed, not assumed away

The available descriptions suggest that the office lease may require notification rather than consent and that Mossvale’s clause may apply to assignment rather than a share sale. Nevertheless, the complete documents should be checked for change-of-control, deemed assignment, termination and default provisions.

Require the Seller to:

- give any required lease notice before Completion and provide evidence;
- warrant that Completion does not trigger termination, default or adverse variation;
- confirm no counterparty has asserted otherwise; and
- obtain consent where full-document review shows it is required.

These appear lower priority than Bluefen but should not be left as interpretive gaps.

---

### 12. Disclosure and warranties must be refreshed at Completion

The disclosure snapshot is as at 22 September 2026. Require:

- an updated data room and disclosure letter;
- continuing notification of new matters;
- warranties repeated at signing and Completion;
- no unilateral supplementary disclosure that removes a Buyer remedy;
- Buyer approval of any new disclosure, with termination, price adjustment or indemnity rights where material; and
- pre-Completion conduct covenants restricting debt, commitments, bonuses, settlements, data notifications and material contract amendments.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

### Completion blockers
1. Clean and unconditional Bluefen consent.
2. Simultaneous Riverlark repayment and security release.
3. Ironquay payment and confirmatory IP assignment.
4. Completed assessment and containment of the privacy incident.
5. Revised funds flow allocating bonuses and on-costs to the Seller.

### Liability and remedy changes
6. Reject application of the 20% cap and 18-month period to title, capacity, tax, IP-specific risks, indemnities, debt, leakage and completion obligations.
7. Reject universal exclusive-remedy, non-reliance and “all Claims” language.
8. Replace general disclosure and constructive knowledge with specific fair disclosure and narrowly defined actual knowledge.
9. Add specific indemnities for Ironquay, the privacy incident, bonuses/on-costs and any failure to discharge Riverlark debt/security.
10. Require stronger general warranty cap/duration and a tipping basket.

### Process and evidence
11. Update and freeze the disclosure record and data-room index.
12. Repeat warranties at Completion and control supplementary disclosure.
13. Obtain robust title deliverables and confirmations regarding leases, Mossvale and supplier renewals.
14. Consider escrow or retention for unresolved privacy/IP exposures and Seller credit risk.

The core commercial message should be that **disclosure alone is not an acceptable solution to known liabilities**. The Seller must cure them before Completion, reflect them in the price mechanics, or provide effective dollar-for-dollar indemnity protection.

- continuing notification of new matters;
- warranties repeated at signing and Completion;
- no unilateral supplementary disclosure that removes a Buyer remedy;
- Buyer approval of any new disclosure, with termination, price adjustment or indemnity rights where material; and
- pre-Completion conduct covenants restricting debt, commitments, bonuses, settlements, data notifications and material contract amendments.

## Recommended negotiation priorities

### Completion blockers
1. Clean and unconditional Bluefen consent.
2. Simultaneous Riverlark repayment and security release.
3. Ironquay payment and confirmatory IP assignment.
4. Completed assessment and containment of the privacy incident.
5. Revised funds flow allocating bonuses and on-costs to the Seller.

### Liability and remedy changes
6. Reject application of the 20% cap and 18-month period to title, capacity, tax, IP-specific risks, indemnities, debt, leakage and completion obligations.
7. Reject universal exclusive-remedy, non-reliance and “all Claims” language.
8. Replace general disclosure and constructive knowledge with specific fair disclosure and narrowly defined actual knowledge.
9. Add specific indemnities for Ironquay, the privacy incident, bonuses/on-costs and any failure to discharge Riverlark debt/security.
10. Require stronger general warranty cap/duration and a tipping basket.

### Process and evidence
11. Update and freeze the disclosure record and data-room index.
12. Repeat warranties at Completion and control supplementary disclosure.
13. Obtain robust title deliverables and confirmations regarding leases, Mossvale and supplier renewals.
14. Consider escrow or retention for unresolved privacy/IP exposures and Seller credit risk.

The core commercial message should be that **disclosure alone is not an acceptable solution to known liabilities**. The Seller must cure them before Completion, reflect them in the price mechanics, or provide effective dollar-for-dollar indemnity protection.
